choices.text: Summit Suites standard queen room, $206/night, 0.4 miles from registration, coffee and mini-fridge listed.
Summit Suites standard king room, $206/night, 0.4 miles from registration, coffee and mini-fridge listed, slightly larger floor plan.
Summit Suites two-double room, $204/night, 0.4 miles from registration, coffee and mini-fridge listed.
Parkview Hotel standard room assigned at check-in, $199/night, 0.3 miles from registration, coffee and mini-fridge listed.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium-hard: the queen and king rooms are the same hotel, price, cancellation window, and room equipment, while the king has ordinary appeal as the larger bed. The distinction turns on Kara's past room-type pattern rather than the visible travel facts.
probes.gold_action: Hold the selectable standard queen room.
probes.label_rationale: Across comparable solo and partner stays, Kara repeatedly chooses or asks to confirm a queen when one larger bed is appropriate, and she avoids two-double or uncertain bed setups before teaching days. A king can be workable, but the pattern does not make it the automatic upgrade over a selectable queen.
probes.query: Kara is making a cancellable hotel hold for a solo Spokane pediatric seating workshop. She will arrive Thursday, teach early Friday and Saturday, and use rideshares. All four choices are in the same conference-area cluster, have similar public ratings, include the same cancellation window, and list in-room coffee plus a mini-fridge. Which room should be put on the hold?

choices.text: Reserve the room tagged deluxe king and note the larger bed and desk area.
Reserve the room tagged one-queen studio and keep the room-equipment confirmation in the note.
Reserve the two-double room at the same rate and note the spare bed for materials.
Reserve the flexible standard room assigned at arrival and add a quiet-floor request.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium-hard: the visible hotel facts are intentionally close, and the king room's larger workspace could look attractive. The correct distinction is the bed-type default Kara has carried across multiple teaching and clinic trips.
probes.gold_action: Select the one-queen studio and document the room equipment.
probes.label_rationale: Kara's recurring booking resolutions favor a queen room or queen studio when the room type can be selected, especially for clinic or course trips with early starts. The alternatives are workable travel products, but king, two-double, and arrival-assigned bedding do not match her settled room setup as closely.
probes.query: Kara is preparing a hotel shortlist for a three-night New Haven children's hospital gait-course visit. She is traveling alone, the host has not locked the hotel, and the four refundable choices are within $8/night, about the same 10-12 minute ride, and rated 4.3-4.4. Each listing shows a desk, in-room coffee, a mini-fridge, and a fitness room. What first-line booking instruction should the planner use?

choices.text: Riverside Lodge king room, full-size mini-fridge and coffee maker, $238/night.
Riverside Lodge queen room, same mini-fridge and coffee maker, $241/night.
Riverside Lodge two-double room, same mini-fridge and coffee maker, $235/night.
Trailhead Hotel run-of-house room, same amenities, $229/night; bed type assigned after check-in.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium-hard: for many couples, the same-property king room would be an obvious competitor, and its price is slightly lower. The past pattern separates queen-as-default from king-as-acceptable rather than making the larger bed the automatic choice.
probes.gold_action: Hold the queen room for the shared one-room stay.
probes.label_rationale: For partner weekends as well as work trips, Kara treats a queen as enough for a one-bed room and pushes away from doubles or uncertain room assignments. A king can be acceptable in some boundary cases, but it is not the reusable first pick when a queen room is directly selectable.
probes.query: Kara and her partner are choosing one refundable room for a Bend trail-and-recovery weekend. The finalists are all in the same downtown-river area, have pool, hot tub, and exercise access, and totals differ by less than $12. Which hold best matches the bed setup to use?

choices.text: Accept the free king upgrade and note that it is the larger one-bed room.
Keep/select the queen studio and leave the king as an optional change only if Kara asks for it.
Switch to the two-double studio so there is a spare bed for course materials.
Use the hotel's bed-assigned-at-arrival option to preserve flexibility until check-in.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium-hard: the queen and king choices are operationally tied, and a free king upgrade is a plausible standard travel move. The deciding factor is the narrow distinction between accepting a king when needed and defaulting to queen when it is selectable.
probes.gold_action: Keep the queen studio rather than treating the free king as the default upgrade.
probes.label_rationale: Kara repeatedly selects or asks for a queen when the room type can be chosen, and she has framed king as not necessary rather than as a standing upgrade target. The free-upgrade prompt is a real competing action, but it should not override the established queen selection.
probes.query: A Springfield, Missouri pediatric lab trip is ready for one refundable room. The hotel Kara had penciled in shows both a queen studio and a same-price king studio with the same coffee maker, mini-fridge, rating, cancellation, and campus shuttle. The booking page is nudging the king as a free upgrade; the current trip notes only say she is traveling alone and teaching early the next morning. What should the planner do at checkout?

choices.text: Official hotel two-double room, connected to sessions, lobby coffee, refrigerator not confirmed, refundable.
Suite hotel queen studio, six-minute covered walk, in-room coffee and mini-fridge confirmed, refundable.
Airport hotel king room, 18-minute ride, in-room coffee and mini-fridge confirmed, refundable.
Downtown boutique run-of-house room, 10-minute ride, lobby coffee and refrigerator by request, refundable.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium-hard: connected access is a strong ordinary-convenience argument, and the rates and ratings do not decide the result. The correct resolution requires balancing the official-location lure against Kara's repeated insistence on confirmed room setup.
probes.gold_action: Lead with the suite hotel queen studio despite the short covered walk.
probes.label_rationale: Kara has repeatedly made confirmed queen setup and in-room basics matter enough to beat a closer official or connected option when the closer room cannot confirm the setup. The connected hotel remains plausible, but the two-double and unconfirmed refrigerator wording are exactly the kind of room friction she tries to avoid before early teaching.
probes.query: For a Worcester pediatric rehab seminar, Kara needs a cancellable two-night room before two 8:00 a.m. teaching blocks. The official hotel is connected to the meeting floor and can offer only a two-double room with lobby coffee and no refrigerator confirmation. A suite hotel a six-minute covered walk away can confirm a queen studio with in-room coffee and a mini-fridge at essentially the same rate and rating. Two other options are shown below. Which hold should lead?

choices.text: Switch to the attached king room because it is slightly cheaper and closer.
Keep the queen-studio hold unless Kara explicitly chooses the attached king tradeoff.
Cancel the hold and wait for a queen room in the block to appear.
Switch to the block's two-double waitlist because attached access matters most.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hard: the attached king has legitimate advantages and does not violate the one-large-bed idea. The distinction is that king is a tolerable fallback or chosen tradeoff, while the recurring default remains the known queen room.
probes.gold_action: Keep the confirmed queen-studio hold rather than switching by default to the attached king room.
probes.label_rationale: Kara's past conference decisions favor staying with a known queen setup when a block or reopened rate cannot match it, even when proximity is tempting. A king room can be acceptable in some cases, but the prior pattern does not support an automatic switch from a confirmed queen to a king solely for a small price or location gain.
probes.query: Kara's Hartford pediatric therapy conference block reopened after a sellout. Her current cancellable hold is a suite-house queen studio eight minutes on foot from registration; it has in-room coffee, a mini-fridge, fitness access, and the same cancellation deadline as the block. The reopened block room is attached to the conference area, costs $6 less, and can confirm a king room with the same room equipment but no queen availability. No one else is sharing the booking. What update should be made?

choices.text: Hospital Garden Inn standard room, bed assigned at arrival, $203/night, closest to the lab.
River Market Suites queen studio, $207/night, short rideshare to the lab.
River Market Suites king studio, $207/night, short rideshare to the lab, slightly larger seating area.
Hospital Garden Inn two-double room, $199/night, closest to the lab.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium-hard: the same-property king studio is equal on price and better on space, while the closest hotel has ordinary location appeal. The bed wording, not a visible price or commute difference, separates the answer.
probes.gold_action: Rank the confirmed queen studio first.
probes.label_rationale: Kara's prior clinic and lab planning distinguishes a confirmed queen from a king, two-double, or arrival-assigned setup. When the commute and room equipment are close enough, the directly selectable queen studio best fits her resolved choices.
probes.query: Kara is building a provisional lodging note for a two-night Little Rock pediatric equipment lab. Four refundable rooms are all within one mile of the hospital, rates are clustered within $10, ratings are 4.2-4.4, and each property lists parking, a desk, in-room coffee, and a mini-fridge. Which room line should be ranked first?

choices.text: Standard king room, with a single larger bed and a slightly bigger desk.
Standard queen room, with the bed type selectable at booking.
Two-queen room, adding a second bed at no extra charge.
Standard room with bed type assigned by the hotel at arrival.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium-hard: all explicit hotel facts are held constant, and the king room has a normal comfort advantage. The result depends on recognizing that Kara's past wording centers on queen specifically when the option is selectable.
probes.label_rationale: Kara's repeated choices point to queen as the selectable one-bed room type, not simply the largest available bed or any room that has at least one bed. The same-rate king and two-queen rooms are viable, but they do not reflect the narrow room-type pattern as well as the standard queen.
probes.query: For a solo Fresno children's-hospital consult, the booking portal asks for a room type before payment. The shortlisted hotel has four refundable room types with the same nightly rate, cancellation terms, customer rating, fitness room, in-room coffee, and mini-fridge. Which selection should be made?

choices.text: Adobe Courtyard queen room, $229/night, two blocks from the meet-up.
Adobe Courtyard king room, $229/night, two blocks from the meet-up, marketed as a complimentary upgrade.
Adobe Courtyard two-double room, $223/night, two blocks from the meet-up.
Mesa View flexible room, $219/night, five blocks from the meet-up; bed type assigned at check-in.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hard: the king room is the same property, same price, same amenities, and presented as an upgrade, making it an attractive near miss. The correct answer requires separating acceptable king fallback from the recurring queen selection.
probes.label_rationale: For one-room partner trips, Kara has repeatedly treated queen as enough and has rejected double-bed setups when a single large bed is the right arrangement. King is acceptable in some boundary cases, but a complimentary upgrade does not become the default over a confirmed queen.
probes.query: Kara and her partner are arranging a Taos active weekend around a Saturday clinic and Sunday recovery hike. They need one refundable room; the four holds have the same cancellation deadline, similar guest scores, onsite parking, a pool, hot tub, exercise room, in-room coffee, and a mini-fridge. Which hold should the planner place?

choices.text: Lakeside Inn confirmed king room, in-room coffee and mini-fridge, pool, hot tub, and fitness room, $246/night.
Lakeside Inn confirmed two-double room, same room equipment and amenities, $242/night.
Lakeside Inn queen waitlist only, no guaranteed bed type if it does not clear, $239/night.
Harbor Annex run-of-house room, bed assigned at check-in, same general area and amenities, $231/night.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hard: the queen waitlist has tempting exact wording and a slightly lower price, while the king room is not the stated default. The distinction is between preferring queen when selectable and using a reliable king when that is the practical one-bed option.
probes.gold_action: Hold the confirmed king room rather than forcing a queen waitlist or choosing doubles.
probes.label_rationale: Kara's pattern supports queen as the recurring first pick, but it also allows a confirmed king for a one-large-bed setup when queen is not available. The boundary is that queen should not be treated as an absolute requirement that pushes the booking into doubles, run-of-house, or a risky waitlist.
probes.query: Kara and her partner need one refundable room for a Traverse City trail weekend, and the preferred inn says every queen room sold out before the hold deadline. These alternatives are all in the same lakeside area with similar guest scores and cancellation windows. Which hold should the planner make tonight?

choices.text: Book the conference hotel's confirmed king room and add a note to switch to queen only if one reopens.
Book the conference hotel's two-double room to stay closest while avoiding the king.
Use the campus inn's queen waitlist and accept whatever room is left if it does not clear.
Book the neighborhood hotel's one-bed-assigned-at-arrival room and wait to learn whether it is queen or king.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hard: an assigned one-bed room could sound close to the desired setup, and the campus queen waitlist has the appealing bed word. The correct handling is to avoid treating queen as mandatory while still avoiding doubles and uncertain assignments.
probes.gold_action: Book the confirmed king room, with a queen switch note only if one reopens.
probes.label_rationale: When an exact queen is unavailable, Kara's past choices favor a confirmed single large bed over doubles or uncertain bedding. King is an acceptable boundary case, especially when it preserves a reliable room setup before a work seminar.
probes.query: A Lexington pediatric mobility seminar has a late hotel change. Before the hold deadline, the conference hotel can confirm either a king room or a two-double room, both with in-room coffee and a mini-fridge; no queen rooms remain. A neighborhood hotel ten minutes away can confirm only one-bed assigned at arrival, and a campus inn has a queen waitlist without a guaranteed hold. The rates and guest scores are close enough for any of them to work. What should the booking note say?

choices.text: Hold the sponsor-cap one-large-bed room, add a queen request, and note that a king assignment is acceptable if that is the guaranteed one-bed room.
Hold the two-double fallback because it can specify an exact bed type within the cap.
Hold the farther queen suite despite the added cost, because queen wording should be mandatory.
Skip the hold and wait for a room that separately names queen under the cap.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hard: the farther suite is the only choice with exact queen wording, so it is a plausible near miss. The correct distinction is that queen should be requested when available, while king remains acceptable within a guaranteed one-large-bed assignment.
probes.gold_action: Hold the guaranteed one-large-bed room, request queen, and allow king if that is the assigned one-bed setup.
probes.label_rationale: Kara's prior choices point to queen as the preferred selectable room type, but the boundary is not to make queen an inflexible requirement when the hotel can guarantee a single large bed and the alternative is doubles, extra cost, or no hold. The added queen request preserves the default without overreading it.
probes.query: For a Santa Rosa pediatric conference add-on, the only hotel inside the sponsor cap cannot lock a queen or king separately, but the front desk will guarantee 'one large bed' and says the assignment will be either queen or king. A nearby fallback can lock two doubles for the same rate, and a farther suite can lock a queen for $32 more per night. All options are refundable and otherwise similar enough for the agenda. Which instruction should the planner use?
